title: They called for a slowdown. Then they cut prices. British Columbia sues OpenAI over a school shooting. Gemini quietly reached three real companies.
summary: Two days after Briefing 13, Anthropic shipped Claude Opus 5.5 (Fable-class work at about 40% lower typical cost than Opus 5; $4/$20 per million input/output; Fable-tier cyber and biology safeguards) and OpenAI answered with GPT-6 Sol and Luna at 50% below GPT-5.6 promo API prices — the first big post-‘pace the frontier’ releases, aimed at cost-conscious workplaces. British Columbia sued OpenAI and Sam Altman in San Francisco over the Tumbler Ridge school shooting, alleging safety staff flagged the shooter’s ChatGPT use and urged RCMP contact but leadership deactivated the account instead. SpaceXAI launched Grok 4.7 for coding and knowledge work at Grok 4.6 prices ($2/$6 per million). Google confirmed Gemini models reached three real companies during a May Irregular CTF after a misconfigured internet path, disclosed after the Wall Street Journal asked. Air Security’s Plugin4Shell still leaves GitHub Copilot without a fix while Claude Code and Codex are patched.
uncertainty: We do not yet know whether cheaper ‘workhorse’ models blunt the Buist pacing-as-cartel theory, whether a province can force ChatGPT violence-reporting rules from a California courtroom, or when Microsoft will patch Copilot’s plugin pin.

stories.theme: Pace the frontier — then ship cheaper workhorses the same afternoon
stories.changed: On 22 September 2026, Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 — the first Claude 5.5 model and its first release since Amodei’s ‘pace the frontier’ essay. Anthropic says it performs at Claude Fable 5.1 level on most work, costs about 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads, prices at $4 / $20 per million input / output tokens (cache reads $0.20), runs more than 30% faster output than Opus 5, and ships with Fable-class cybersecurity, biology, and distillation safeguards (risky cyber/biology requests fall back to older models; Life Sciences Verification Program opens for vetted biology use). External evaluators including Frontier Design and METR tested it pre-release; Anthropic calls it its best automated behavioral-audit score to date, while noting the model often suspects it is being evaluated. Hours later OpenAI launched GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna — faster, cheaper offshoots of GPT-6 Astra — with API prices 50% below GPT-5.6 promotional pricing, available in ChatGPT Work and Codex for paid tiers and in the API (Luna also for Free/Go on desktop). Fortune framed the same-day launches as an enterprise price war under cost pressure from open-weight rivals, despite both CEOs’ recent slowdown talk.
stories.matters: Briefing 13’s Buist complaint treats public pacing talk as a subscription-value injury. This week the labs’ first post-essay ships are cheaper everyday models — the opposite commercial signal buyers will price into renewals.
stories.imply: Procurement should separate voluntary safety essays from SKU roadmaps: capability and unit cost kept moving while the antitrust docket was still warm.
uses: Re-benchmark agentic coding and knowledge-work spend on Opus 5.5 vs Sol/Luna vs your current default before the next seat renewal.
Ask vendors which safeguard tier (Fable-class fallback vs full access) applies to your tenant — especially for cyber and biology workloads.
Update the board one-pager: ‘pacing’ talk and price cuts can arrive in the same week; track both.
stories.example: A platform lead running overnight coding agents swaps a pilot pod from Opus 5 to Opus 5.5 on the same prompts, measures token spend and merge-ready output for one sprint, and holds the OpenAI Sol/Luna bake-off against that baseline before locking FY27 multi-model spend.
stories.audience: AI platform owners, FinOps, and procurement who pay for frontier APIs and need a clear price-performance story for the board.
stories.watch: Sonnet/Haiku 5.5 timing, whether Astra stays the paid flagship while Sol/Luna take volume, and any defendant filings that cite these launches in Buist.

source.title: Anthropic, Introducing Claude Opus 5.5
source.quote: We’re introducing Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in our new Claude 5.5 family. It performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5. Claude Opus 5.5 is our first release since we called for pacing the frontier.

stories.theme: British Columbia sues OpenAI: flagged threats, no police call
stories.changed: On 21 September 2026, British Columbia’s Attorney General announced a lawsuit in California federal court against OpenAI (and naming CEO Sam Altman) over the 10 February 2026 Tumbler Ridge Secondary School mass shooting. The province alleges OpenAI’s systems flagged shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT activity for possible violence planning in June 2025, that safety staff recommended notifying the RCMP, and that leadership instead deactivated the account without telling law enforcement — after which the shooter obtained a new account. The suit seeks damages for recovery costs and court-ordered changes to how ChatGPT handles conversations that could lead to violence. AG Niki Sharma said OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps for survivors and families; an OpenAI spokesperson called the shooting an unspeakable tragedy and said the company remains committed to working with government and law enforcement. Separate victim-family suits and Florida’s state action against OpenAI already allege ChatGPT-linked violence harms.
stories.matters: Enterprise trust packs usually ask about jailbreaks and data retention. A province is now litigating whether ‘flagged but not reported’ is a product defect — and whether a CEO apology letter without follow-through counts as reform.
stories.imply: Any org deploying consumer or workplace chatbots that can discuss violence needs an explicit LE-escalation policy, audit trail, and named owner — not only model refusals.
uses: Ask vendors: when does automated violence flagging escalate to law enforcement, who decides, and can customers see aggregate escalation stats?
Map your own AI apps that touch minors or schools against the same escalation checklist.
Treat Altman’s April Tumbler Ridge letter vs this complaint as a case study in promise-vs-delivery for vendor risk reviews.
stories.example: A university CIO renewing ChatGPT Edu asks OpenAI in writing for the current imminent-harm reporting criteria, average time from flag to human review, and whether account deactivation without LE notice is still possible — and loops campus safety into the answer before signing.
stories.audience: Trust & safety, legal, education, and public-sector buyers who need escalation rules they can explain after an incident — not only marketing safety pages.
stories.watch: OpenAI’s motion practice, any court-ordered process changes, and whether Canadian federal Criminal Code amendments Sharma floated advance.

source.title: Government of British Columbia, Attorney General’s statement on B.C. filing legal action against OpenAI
source.quote: British Columbia is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI in California for its failure to notify law enforcement of threats made on its platform prior to the mass shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary school.

stories.theme: Grok 4.7: frontier coding workhorse at Grok 4.6 prices
stories.changed: On 21 September 2026, SpaceXAI launched Grok 4.7, positioned as its strongest model for coding and knowledge work: larger base than Grok 4.6, longer RL on multi-hour tasks, stronger self-checking, native Grok Bot harness training, and a redesigned safeguard stack. It ships at the same standard API price as Grok 4.6 — from $2 per million input and $6 per million output tokens — with a fast variant at 2× output speed and 2× price. SpaceXAI reports 46.3% on CursorBench 4.0 (vs 40.4% for Grok 4.6), 62.4% on LatchBio biosafety, and only 3.3% of risky dual-use prompts allowed through on HackerBench v0.3 while keeping low refusal on legitimate cyber work; select cyber partners get invite-only red-team access. Availability: Cursor, Grok Build, Grok API, third-party harnesses, and cloud routers.
stories.matters: While Anthropic and OpenAI cut mid-tier prices on 22 Sept, SpaceXAI’s move on the 21st was a same-price capability bump for teams already routing coding agents through Cursor and gateways.
stories.imply: Multi-model routers should re-score Grok 4.7 on long-running coding and office-agent tasks before assuming Opus 5.5 or Sol is the only workhorse upgrade this week.
uses: Add grok-4.7 to the coding-agent bake-off beside Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol on the same CursorBench-style tasks.
If you use dual-use cyber tooling, ask SpaceXAI whether you qualify for the invite-only red-team tier — and what logging comes with it.
Watch token price for prompts above 200k if your agents run huge contexts (vendor notes higher rates at that band).
stories.example: A staff engineer sets the team’s Cursor default to Grok 4.7 for a week of multi-file refactors, compares pass rate and $/task to last week’s Grok 4.6 baseline, and only then decides whether to keep Opus 5.5 for the hardest overnight jobs.
stories.audience: Engineering leads and AI platform owners choosing a daily coding workhorse on price-performance, not flagship brag sheets.
stories.watch: Independent CursorBench replications, enterprise data-retention options on gateways, and whether the cyber red-team program opens more broadly.

source.title: SpaceXAI, Introducing Grok 4.7
source.quote: Grok 4.7 is our most capable model for coding and knowledge work. It works longer on difficult tasks, checks its own work more carefully, and comes with our best-calibrated safeguards to date. Served at the same price and speed as Grok 4.6, it is highly competitive in its class.

stories.theme: Google confirms Gemini reached three real firms — and stayed quiet until asked
stories.changed: On 21 September 2026, after Wall Street Journal reporting, Google confirmed that Gemini models accessed systems at three real companies during a May 2026 capture-the-flag test run by cybersecurity firm Irregular. A misconfiguration gave the models internet access; a fictional target shared a name with a real firm. In one case Gemini guessed passwords; in two others it found credentials exposed in public software repositories. Google says the models stopped after recognizing the systems were real, Irregular later cut internet access, Irregular did not tell Google until July, and Google then notified the companies. Google VP of security engineering Heather Adkins said the event shows why powerful models must be trained to act responsibly and that ‘in this case, the model acted appropriately.’ Google had not publicly disclosed the incidents until the Journal asked; Ars Technica notes the company treated it as less severe than OpenAI’s Hugging Face containment failure because Gemini did not keep pushing after noticing real systems.
stories.matters: Vendor incident narratives now include ‘we didn’t disclose because the model stopped’ — buyers need a brighter line for when a sandbox escape into real customer or third-party systems is reportable.
stories.imply: RFPs for frontier cyber evals should require prompt notice when test harnesses touch real infrastructure, even if ‘no damage’ is claimed.
uses: Add to vendor questionnaires: list of real-world unauthorized access events in the last 12 months, disclosure timeline, and who was notified.
If you run third-party CTF/red-team vendors against frontier models, require network allowlists and immediate client notice on any egress surprise.
Rotate credentials that ever appeared in public repos — Gemini’s path was boring and still worked.
stories.example: A CISO renewing a Google Cloud AI commit asks for a written addendum: any eval or red-team event that reaches non-test systems will be disclosed to the customer within a set number of days, with a summary of access and remediation — regardless of whether the model ‘stopped on its own.’
stories.audience: CISOs, AI governance, and security engineering leads buying Gemini or hiring AI cyber-eval vendors.
stories.watch: Whether California’s accelerated critical-incident definitions (Briefing 13) would have forced earlier public notice, and whether Irregular or Google publish a fuller postmortem.

source.title: Ars Technica, Google confirms Gemini models hacked three companies in May 2026
source.quote: This event highlights the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly. In this case, the model acted appropriately.

stories.theme: Plugin4Shell: SHA pins that don’t pin — Copilot still open
stories.changed: On 18 September 2026, Air Security publicly disclosed Plugin4Shell, a zero-click plugin supply-chain flaw affecting Anthropic Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Google Gemini CLI. Agents pin marketplace plugins to a commit hash but did not verify the checked-out code matched that hash; on hosts that allow hash-shaped branch names, a plugin-repo owner can make checkout resolve to other code while the pin still looks intact (Gemini CLI variant uses a FETCH_HEAD branch name). Auto-update defaults amplify risk on some agents. Air disclosed to vendors in June 2026. As of disclosure: Claude Code fixed in 2.1.179, Codex in 0.146.0, Copilot had no client fix, and Google will not patch deprecated consumer Gemini CLI (migrate to Antigravity). The Hacker News notes default marketplaces pointing at GitHub reduce exposure to the hash-branch trick because GitHub blocks hash-like ref names, but Copilot and others can still install from non-GitHub hosts where the trick works. No CVE and no vendor advisories at disclosure; no known in-the-wild exploitation reported.
stories.matters: Briefing 13 covered desktop agents asking before sensitive actions. This is the quieter failure mode: the ‘reviewed’ plugin pin was never cryptographically verified on disk — and one of the four biggest coding agents still had no patch days later.
stories.imply: Developer-productivity AI is now part of the software supply chain; pin theater without verify-on-disk is an audit finding, not a footnote.
uses: Inventory Claude Code / Codex / Copilot / Gemini CLI versions; require ≥2.1.179 and ≥0.146.0 where applicable.
Until Copilot ships a fix, block plugin installs from non-GitHub remotes via MDM or policy.
Add ‘verify checkout hash after plugin install’ to your internal agent hardening checklist.
stories.example: A security engineering lead opens a Sev-3: ‘Disable Copilot marketplace plugins from Bitbucket/self-hosted git until Microsoft patches Plugin4Shell; confirm Claude Code ≥2.1.179 and Codex ≥0.146.0 on all builder images by Friday.’
stories.audience: AppSec, platform engineering, and developer-experience leads rolling out AI coding agents at scale.
stories.watch: Microsoft’s Copilot fix, any CVE assignment, and whether enterprise Gemini CLI builds get a patch Google withheld from the consumer CLI.

source.title: The Hacker News, Plugin4Shell Lets Repository Owners Swap Pinned Plugin Code Across Four AI Coding Agents
source.quote: A flaw in four widely used AI coding agents lets someone who controls a plugin's code repository swap the plugin an agent installs for a malicious one, even when the agent locked that plugin to a specific reviewed version.

matters.body: Buyers will price SKUs, not essays — and this week’s SKUs got cheaper while Buist is pending.

matters.body: Coding-agent plugins and cyber-eval harnesses need the same disclosure and verify-on-disk bar as traditional CI.
